modules.name: Universal Audio Processor
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; LGE208 version by Low-Gain Electronics
modules.summary: Two VCAs with an equal-power control circuit, switchable between a dual VCA, a stereo panner and a voltage-controlled crossfader.
how_it_works: Inside are two voltage-controlled amplifiers and a small control circuit that drives them. The control circuit makes two complementary control signals: as one VCA opens, the other closes. Because the curve is equal-power rather than linear, the overall loudness stays the same as a sound moves between the two sides, with no dip in the middle.
The three-position switch changes how the audio is routed between the two VCAs, so one panel does three jobs without any patching:

PAN (up): one input signal feeds both VCAs. PAN / FADE and VC PAN move it between OUT 1 and OUT 2: a stereo panner. GAIN and VC 1+2 set the overall level. The arrows on the panel show which input is shared in each mode.
DUAL VCA (centre): the two VCAs work on their own. IN 1 goes to OUT 1 under VC 1, IN 2 to OUT 2 under VC 2: two separate amplifiers for envelopes, tremolo or gating.
XFADE (down): two different signals at IN 1 and IN 2 are blended under voltage control. PAN / FADE and VC PAN set the mix, and as one source rises the other falls.
AM 1 and AM 2 are AC-coupled inputs for amplitude modulation at audio rates, separate from the DC-coupled VC inputs. Each output appears on both a 1/4" jack and a banana.
controls: Each output on a 1/4" jack and a banana jack.
Audio inputs; their routing follows the mode switch.

Control of the pan or crossfade position.
Control of both VCAs together (overall level).

modules.name: VC Phaser
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS90 version by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A voltage-controlled phase shifter with three phase-shifted outputs and a built-in mix for the classic notched phasing sound.
how_it_works: The input runs through a chain of all-pass stages. An all-pass stage leaves the level of every frequency alone but delays its phase, and the amount of delay depends on frequency and on the control voltage. Taps along the chain give outputs shifted by 360°, 720° and 1080°.

On their own the shifted outputs sound almost the same as the input, because the ear hardly hears phase. The effect appears when a shifted signal is mixed back with the original: frequencies that come out of phase cancel, cutting a row of notches into the spectrum. The MIXED output does this inside the module with the 1080° tap, and the MIX knob sets the balance.
PHASE sets the shift by hand. The VC input, through its attenuator, sweeps it from an envelope, LFO or sequencer; the response follows a log curve so sweeps sound even across the range.

Ken Stone's CGS90 puts two small audio mixers on the same PCB. Each has three inputs with level knobs plus one unity-gain x1 input. They are inverting and AC coupled, which makes them good for blending the raw phase outputs with the dry signal (straight or inverted) and for feedback patches: mix the phaser's output with its input before it goes back in. Patch one mixer's output into the other's x1 input to get a single six-input mixer.
controls: Input mixed with the 1080° output: the phasing sound.
Audio in. The CGS90 panel has two IN jacks.
Control voltage for the amount of shift, with attenuator.
CGS90 only: two inverting audio mixers, three level-controlled inputs and one unity-gain input each.

modules.name: Wave Multipliers
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS113 version by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Three separate voltage-controlled waveshapers that add harmonics to a signal instead of filtering them away.
how_it_works: A filter changes timbre by removing frequencies. The Wave Multipliers do the opposite: they bend the waveform so that new, harmonically related overtones appear. Each of the three sections works in a different way, and each has its own control voltage and knob. In a VCO-VCF-VCA patch the usual place for it is between the oscillator and the filter.

Top section: a switch picks the mode. In HI it squares up the signal with rounded, saturated peaks, like an overdriven tube amplifier but voltage controlled. In LO it is a plain linear VCA, handy for amplitude modulation or for gating a signal into the other sections.

Middle section: fed with a sine wave, turning it up sweeps through the odd harmonics, up to about the 13th. It sounds like overblowing a pipe closed at one end, so it suits reed and wind sounds. A second input lets two signals be mixed before processing, which gives sum-and-difference-like effects richer than a ring modulator.

Bottom section: chained full-wave rectifiers, each of which doubles the frequency of a sine or triangle. Sweeping the control moves smoothly through the even harmonics (2nd, 4th, 8th) without the drop in level a plain rectifier gives. It has two inputs and two outputs; the second output is a squared-up version of the first and behaves like a more complex pulse-width modulation.
controls: Control voltage and manual amount for that section.
Top section: linear VCA (LO) or soft squaring (HI).
Middle and bottom sections: two inputs mixed before processing.
Processed signals; OUT 2 of the bottom section is the squared version.
related: The Wave Multipliers, Wave Multiplier (1") and Wave Multiplier 2in panels in the CGS folder come from The Human Comparator artwork and are different circuits.

modules.name: Dual Universal Slope Generator
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS114 version by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Two identical slope generators, each of which can be a slew limiter, envelope, LFO, audio oscillator or pulse divider.
how_it_works: Each half produces a voltage that rises and falls at rates set by the RISE and FALL knobs. What it does depends only on what is patched into it.

Slew: a voltage at IN is followed by the output, but no faster than the RISE and FALL times allow. With a stepped voltage at IN this gives portamento; with the knobs fully up the output simply copies the input.
Envelope: a pulse at TRIG IN starts a rise from 0 to about +5 V followed by the fall. A new trigger during the envelope is ignored, and an END pulse comes out when the cycle finishes.

Oscillator: patch END back to TRIG IN (or set the cycle switch where fitted) and the slope runs continuously, from slow LFO up to audio. With RISE and FALL equal it makes a triangle; making one much shorter turns it into a sawtooth.

Pitch and control: 1V/OCT halves the rise and fall times for each added volt, so the slope tracks a keyboard. VC IN, through its attenuator, varies the times too, and the switch chooses whether VC acts on RISE, FALL or BOTH.
Divider: feed a pulse train into TRIG IN with a cycle a little longer than the pulse spacing, and the generator skips pulses, producing sub-harmonics.
controls: Pulse at the end of each cycle (LED shows activity).
Control of the times, with attenuator.

modules.name: Oscillator (1973)
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin, 1973
modules.summary: The original paperface VCO: a sine-to-saw waveshaper under voltage control, two frequency inputs, hard sync and AC / DC outputs.
how_it_works: A single voltage-controlled oscillator. Its waveshaper morphs the output smoothly from sine to sawtooth, set by the WAVE SHAPE knob and its voltage control.
Two frequency control inputs, each with its own level knob, set the pitch: use one for a keyboard or sequencer and the other for frequency modulation.
A sync input hard-syncs the oscillator to another. The outputs come both AC coupled (for audio) and DC coupled (for use as a control voltage).

modules.name: VC Filter (1973)
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin, 1973; CGS77 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A two-pole state-variable resonant filter with simultaneous low-pass, band-pass and high-pass outputs.
how_it_works: A state-variable filter: one circuit produces low-pass, band-pass and high-pass versions of the input at the same time, each on its own output. All three share one cutoff frequency and one resonance (Q).
The cutoff is set by a knob and by voltage control; Q sets how strongly the filter rings at the cutoff. The original uses CA3080 transconductance amplifiers for the voltage-controlled stages.
Prism's calibration starts with a sawtooth into the audio input and the cutoff fully down, listening at the low-pass output.
controls: High-pass, band-pass and low-pass at once.

modules.name: Triple Comparator
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS96 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Three comparators for squaring signals, variable-width pulses, level detection and amplitude-based logic.
how_it_works: Each section compares two voltages and switches its output high or low according to which is larger. Fed with a waveform and a reference, it produces a square or pulse wave whose width moves as the reference moves.
The reference can be a fixed voltage, a slowly changing control voltage, or another audio signal, so the comparators also serve as level detectors and for logic decisions based on amplitude.

modules.name: Triple Wave Shaper
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS85 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Three non-linear waveshapers that turn a sawtooth into a sine and, chained, fold waves into richer shapes.
how_it_works: Each section bends the input waveform through a non-linear curve. With the right level a sawtooth or triangle comes out close to a sine wave; driven harder, the peaks fold back.
The three sections are independent, but patched in series each one adds another fold, building up brighter and more complex timbres. They work on oscillators and on external signals from a preamp.

modules.name: Ring Modulator
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS79 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: An AC or DC coupled ring modulator with voltage control that moves between full ring modulation and amplitude modulation.
how_it_works: Two signals, X and Y, are multiplied. With both as audio the output holds their sum and difference frequencies: the metallic, bell-like ring-mod sound. With one as a slow control voltage it becomes a VCA.
Two VC inputs move the module smoothly between full ring modulation and plain amplitude modulation. DC coupling lets it process control voltages as well as audio.

modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS82 by Ken Stone

modules.name: Smooth & Stepped Generator
aka: Smooth Function / Stepped Function VC Generator
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS92 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A Smooth (slew) section and a Stepped (track-and-hold) section that couple together for random voltages, portamento and oscillators.
how_it_works: The Smooth section slews any voltage in both directions under voltage control: lag, portamento, or a low-frequency filter. Patch its CYCLE jack to its input and it oscillates as a voltage-controlled triangle oscillator.
The Stepped section samples its input and holds the value, moving in steps at a rate set by its own control.

The COUPLER links the two halves. Coupled to each other they make smooth or stepped random voltages, staircase waves and many other patterns, which is why the SSG is one of the most patched Serge modules.

modules.name: Peak & Trough
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS84 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Analog logic: the Peak side passes the highest of its inputs (analog OR), the Trough side the lowest (analog AND).
how_it_works: Each side takes several voltages at once. PEAK outputs whichever input is highest at each moment; TROUGH outputs whichever is lowest.
With gates these act as OR and AND; with audio or slow voltages they combine shapes in ways a mixer cannot, such as clipping one waveform with another or picking the louder of two envelopes.

modules.name: Analog Shift Register
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS34 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A three-stage bucket-brigade sample-and-hold: each clock pulse passes every held voltage on to the next output.
how_it_works: On each clock pulse the first stage samples the input, and each stage hands its held voltage to the next. The outputs give the current value and the two before it, so a single melody turns into a three-part canon.
A built-in gate-to-trigger converter gives its own pulse output for clocking other modules. Some resistor pairs need matching for accuracy.

modules.name: Noise Source
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS97 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: White and pink noise plus a sample-and-hold source for random voltages, triggered by pulses or a push button.
how_it_works: A noise transistor produces white noise; a filter shapes it into pink noise. Both appear on their own outputs.
The S/H source feeds a sample-and-hold so that each trigger, from a pulse or the panel button, gives a new equally probable random voltage.

modules.name: Dual Processor
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin
modules.summary: Two circuits that add, scale and invert control voltages, each with three inputs and a manual offset.
how_it_works: Each half sums three input voltages. Each input has a level control that also sets polarity, so a voltage can be added, reduced or inverted.
A manual offset adds a fixed voltage to the result. Use it to combine envelopes and LFOs, transpose a sequence, or turn a 0-5 V signal into a bipolar one.
controls: Amount and polarity of each input.
Manual voltage added to the sum.

modules.name: Dual Mixer
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin
modules.summary: Two mixers, each with three level-controlled inputs and one unity-gain input.
how_it_works: Each section sums three inputs through level knobs plus one input at fixed unity gain. Chain one section's output into the other's unity input to make a single larger mixer.
Outputs can be built as 1/4", 3.5 mm or banana jacks; mixing a module's output back into its own input makes useful feedback patches.

modules.name: Sequencer (Ten-Stage Pulse Sequencer)
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin
modules.summary: A ten-stage pulse sequencer with CLOCK, RESET and HOLD inputs and a pulse output per stage.
how_it_works: Each clock pulse moves the sequencer one stage on. The active stage puts out a pulse (and lights its LED), so the stages fire other modules in turn: envelopes, routers, sample-and-holds or a Programmer.
RESET returns it to the first stage and HOLD freezes it, so sequences of fewer than ten steps and stop-start patterns are easy. Prism's calibration sets the step output to 5-6 V.

modules.name: X-Fader
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin
modules.summary: A voltage-controlled crossfader between two signals, with a built-in VCA on the result.
how_it_works: Two inputs are blended into one output. A knob sets the starting balance and a control voltage moves it, so one source fades out as the other fades in.
A VCA on the output sets the overall level with its own knob and control input. AC or DC coupling lets it crossfade audio or control voltages.

modules.name: Gate Sequencer
modules.designer: Ken Stone (CGS89), after the Serge paperface Gate Sequencer
modules.summary: A step sequencer of gates: each stage sends its pulse to a chosen output row.
how_it_works: A counter steps through the stages on each clock. A switch at each stage sends that stage's gate to one of the output rows or leaves it silent, giving rhythmic patterns across several outputs.
This is Ken Stone's smaller-format version; the original paperface Gate Sequencer is a different panel (photo still needed).

modules.name: Extended ADSR
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS116 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A voltage-controlled ADSR with an extra stage, keyboard tracking and a shape switch.
how_it_works: GATE and TRIG start the envelope; each stage has its own voltage-control input and knob, so the envelope's shape can be modulated while it plays.
1V/OCT (or VC ALL) scales all the stages together so envelopes get shorter as notes get higher. A switch picks the envelope shape, and an LED shows activity.

modules.name: Extended Range VCF / Variable Q VCF
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS112 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Serge's resonant voltage-controlled filter with low, high, band and notch outputs over a very wide range.
how_it_works: A resonant filter with low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and notch outputs. Q can be set high enough to ring or oscillate; VC Q and VC F control resonance and frequency.
Ken Stone's CGS112 builds it from three CGS108 Serge gain cells on a carrier board. The gain-cell schematic is not published.
